entries.name: Monoid
entries.summary:
Types whose values combine associatively and have a neutral element.

Implemented by `Integer` (addition), `String` and `List` (concatenation), `Map` and both `Set` flavours (union), and `Ordering` ("first decision wins" — declared beside `Ordering` in `comparable.kex`).

entries.name: identity
entries.summary:
The neutral element: combining it with any value gives that value back.

`combine` must be associative and `identity` neutral on both sides.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary:
Combines this value with `other`.

Must be associative: `a.combine(b).combine(c)` and `a.combine(b.combine(c))` have to agree.

entries.name: repeat
entries.summary:
Combines this value with itself `n` times.

Repeating zero times gives the identity: `""` for a string, `0` for an integer, `[]` for a list. A negative count is invalid and ends the program.

entries.name: Group
entries.summary:
A `Monoid` in which every value has an inverse that combines with it to give the identity.

Implemented by `Integer`, where the inverse is negation.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: The neutral element.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Combines this value with `other`.

entries.name: inverse
entries.summary: The value that combines with this one to give the identity.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary: Implements `Monoid`, `Group` over `Integer` for addition.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: `0`: the neutral element for addition.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Adds `other` to this integer. Addition is the monoid operation for `Integer`.

entries.name: inverse
entries.summary: The additive inverse: this integer negated.

entries.name: String
entries.summary: Implements `Monoid` over `String` for concatenation.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: `""`: the neutral element for concatenation.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Concatenates `other` onto this string. Concatenation is the monoid operation for `String`.

entries.name: [A]
entries.summary: Implements `Monoid` over `List<A>` for concatenation.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: `[]`: the neutral element for concatenation.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Concatenates `other` onto this list. Concatenation is the monoid operation for `List`.

entries.name: Atom
entries.summary:
Atoms: the `:name` values. An atom is its own name — two atoms with the same text are the same value, and comparing them is as cheap as comparing numbers.

```kex
:ok
:b@localhost                  # an interior `@` is part of a bare atom
:"b@host.example.com"         # the quoted form spells any text
```

Most atoms are written in the source. From text:

```kex
"hello".as(Atom)     # at compile time, from a literal
Atom.from(text)      # at run time, making the atom — a node name, say
text.to(Atom)        # at run time, only an atom that already exists: Atom?
```

and `string` gives the text back.

entries.name: from
entries.summary:
Returns the atom whose name is `text`.

On the BEAM atoms are never freed, and a node holds at most about a million. Build atoms from a bounded set of names — node names, config keys — never from untrusted input; `text.to(Atom)` is the safe form for that, since it only finds atoms that already exist.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the atom's name as text, without the leading colon. Total, like `Char.string`: every atom has a name.

entries.name: Binary
entries.summary:
An opaque, immutable sequence of bytes. A `Binary` never implicitly becomes text.

`[Byte]` is the materialized list of bytes, while `Binary` is the storage form. A file, an HTTP body, or a digest is a `Binary`. On the BEAM it is a native binary, so slicing shares storage instead of copying. None of the operations here walks a character list.

```kex
let data = Binary.fromHex("00686900").try
data.length            # => 4
data.at(1)             # => Just(104)
data.take(2).hex       # => "0068"
data.showValue         # => "#Binary<4 bytes>"
```

The type is opaque on purpose: there is no field to reach through, so text operations cannot be run on bytes by accident. Conversions are always explicit in both directions, and both directions can fail. Runtime conversions through `to` always return an `Optional<T>`:

```kex
"árvíz".to(Binary)                  #  => Just(#Binary<7 bytes>) : Binary?
Binary.fromBytes([255]).to(String)  # => None
```

`Showable` and `Inspectable` deliberately render the length alone. Neither ever decodes or interpolates the payload, so printing a binary cannot leak its contents or fail on bytes that are not text. Use `hex`, `base64`, or `to(String)` when you actually want to see it.

entries.name: empty
entries.summary:
The binary holding no bytes.

Backed by `Binary.fromBytes([])`, this is the natural starting value this library uses, just like (`Headers.empty`).

entries.name: fromBytes
entries.summary:
Builds a binary from a list of bytes.

Total: every `Byte` is in `0..255` by construction, so there is no rejection case. `Binary.fromBytes([])` is the empty binary.

entries.name: fromHex
entries.summary:
Decodes lowercase hexadecimal text.

Strict, so that decoding is the exact inverse of `hex`: uppercase digits, an odd length, whitespace, a `0x` prefix, and any non-hex character all answer `None` rather than being repaired.

entries.name: fromBase64
entries.summary:
Decodes standard base64 text (RFC 4648).

Strict, so that decoding is the exact inverse of `base64`: the URL-safe alphabet, missing or malformed padding, whitespace, and any other noncanonical encoding all answer `None`.

entries.name: bytes
entries.summary:
The bytes, as a list.

The explicit, allocating conversion out of binary storage. Reach for `length`, `at`, `take`, and `drop` when you do not need the whole list.

entries.name: length
entries.summary: Number of bytes held.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary: Whether it holds no bytes at all.

entries.name: at
entries.summary:
The byte at `index`, counting from zero.

Answers `None` for a negative or out-of-range index, so an index you did not check is something you handle rather than something that stops the program.

entries.name: get
entries.summary: The byte at `index`, counting from zero. The same as `at`, matching the `get` that `List` and `String` carry.

entries.name: take
entries.summary:
The first `count` bytes.

Clamped at both ends, like the list operations: a `count` of zero or less answers the empty binary, and an oversized one answers the whole binary.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary:
Everything after the first `count` bytes.

Clamped at both ends: a `count` of zero or less answers the whole binary, and an oversized one answers the empty binary. `take(n)` and `drop(n)` therefore always concatenate back to the original.
Joins two binaries end to end.

entries.name: hex
entries.summary: The bytes as lowercase hexadecimal text, two digits per byte.

entries.name: base64
entries.summary: The bytes as standard base64 text (RFC 4648), with canonical padding.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: The length-only rendering: never the payload.

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary: The length-only rendering: never the payload. The same as `showValue`.

entries.name: to
entries.summary:
Decodes the payload as UTF-8, or answers `None` when the bytes are not valid text.

This deliberately differs from `showValue`, which reveals only the byte count. Converting asks to inspect the actual payload and therefore makes the possibility of invalid text explicit.

entries.name: Bits
entries.summary:
Bitwise operations on `Integer`.

```kex
Bits.and(0xff, 0x0f)      # => 15
Bits.shiftLeft(1, 8)      # => 256
Bits.test?(0b1010, 1)     # => true
```

Useful for packing flags into one number, reading a binary format, or working with a protocol that describes its fields in bits.

Integers are arbitrary precision, and a negative one behaves as if it were written in infinite-precision two's complement, so `Bits.not(0)` is `-1` and `Bits.and(-1, 255)` is `255`, with no word size to overflow. Shifts and bit indices count from bit 0 (the least significant bit).

entries.name: and
entries.summary: Bitwise AND of `a` and `b`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary: Bitwise OR of `a` and `b`.

entries.name: xor
entries.summary: Bitwise exclusive OR of `a` and `b`.

entries.name: not
entries.summary: Bitwise complement of `a`. Every integer is signed and unbounded, so this is always +-(a + 1)+ rather than a width-dependent mask.

entries.name: shiftLeft
entries.summary: Shifts `n` left by `by` bits. Raises if `by` is negative.

entries.name: shiftRight
entries.summary: Shifts `n` right by `by` bits, propagating the sign: the result of shifting a negative number stays negative. Raises if `by` is negative.

entries.name: test?
entries.summary: True when the bit at `index` of `n` is set. Raises if `index` is negative.

entries.name: set
entries.summary: `n` with the bit at `index` set. Raises if `index` is negative.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary: `n` with the bit at `index` cleared. Raises if `index` is negative.

entries.name: toggle
entries.summary: `n` with the bit at `index` flipped. Raises if `index` is negative.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Number of set bits in `n` (population count). A negative value has infinitely many under two's complement, so this raises for one.

entries.name: width
entries.summary: Number of bits needed to represent `n`, i.e. the position of its highest set bit plus one. Zero needs none. Raises for a negative value.

entries.name: Blankable
entries.summary:
`Blankable`: types that can be asked whether they hold anything meaningful.

A value is blank when it has no meaningful content: `None`, an empty or all-whitespace string, an empty collection, or `false`. The semantics are Rails's, and the point is the same: one question that works across types, so a validation does not need a different test per field.

```kex
"".blank?        # => true
"   ".blank?     # => true   (unlike "   ".empty?)
[].blank?        # => true
None.blank?      # => true
"hi".present?    # => true
```

`present?` is the negation, and is often what reads better:

```kex
fields.all? { |name, value| value.present? }
```

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the value holds nothing meaningful.

What that means is up to each type: whitespace-only for a string, no elements for a collection, `None` for an optional, `false` for a boolean.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for `false`: the only blank boolean.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Always `false`: every integer is a value, including zero.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Always `false`: every float is a value, including zero.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the string is empty or contains only whitespace.

This is what separates it from `empty?`: a string of spaces is not empty, but it is blank, and for user input that is usually the question being asked.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for `None` and `false` for a `Just`: whatever it wraps.

Note that `Just("")` is present, not blank: the optional holds a value, even though that value is itself blank.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the list has no elements.

entries.name: Ordering
entries.summary:
The result of a comparison: `Less`, `Equal` or `Greater`.

Declared here rather than only inside the interpreter so that `Ordering`, `Less`, `Equal` and `Greater` reach the semantic layer the same way every other stdlib type does (through the collected interfaces) instead of existing solely as native environment bindings the type checker and name resolver cannot see.

entries.name: Comparable
entries.summary:
Types that have a total order.

Implemented by `Number`, which covers both `Integer` and `Float`, and by `String`.

entries.name: compare
entries.summary:
Compares this value with `other` and answers `Less`, `Equal` or `Greater`.

`==` stays independent of this: a type may be equatable without being ordered.

A total order: `compare` answers Less, Equal or Greater. `==` stays independent: a type may be Equatable without being ordered.

entries.name: Number
entries.summary: Number carries the implementation, so Integer and Float both inherit it rather than repeating the same three comparisons. Mixed receivers work because `<` and `>` promote across the two (`1.compare(1.0)` is Equal).

entries.name: compare
entries.summary:
Compares two numbers, across the `Integer`/`Float` boundary.

Mixed receivers work because `<` and `>` promote across the two, so `1.compare(1.0)` is `Equal`.

entries.name: String
entries.summary: Strings order lexicographically, character by character, by code point — the same order `<` and `>` already give them.

entries.name: compare
entries.summary: Compares this string with `other` lexicographically, the same order `<` and `>` give strings.

entries.name: Ordering
entries.summary:
`Ordering` is a Monoid under "first decision wins", with Equal as identity. That is what makes multi-key comparison compose instead of nesting ifs:

```kex
a.name.compare(b.name).combine(a.age.compare(b.age))
```

`combine` evaluates its argument eagerly, so the later comparison runs even when the earlier one already decided. Use `thenBy` when that matters.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: `Equal` is the neutral element, since an undecided comparison lets the next one decide.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary:
Returns the first decisive ordering: this one if it is not `Equal`, otherwise `other`.

This is what makes multi-key comparison compose. Note that `other` is evaluated eagerly, so the later comparison runs even when the earlier one has already decided: use `thenBy` when that matters.

entries.name: reverse
entries.summary:
Returns the opposite ordering: `Less` becomes `Greater`, `Greater` becomes `Less`, and `Equal` stays `Equal`.

The one-word way to turn an ascending comparison into a descending one.

entries.name: thenBy
entries.summary:
Returns this ordering if it is decisive, otherwise the result of calling `tieBreaker`.

The short-circuiting form of `combine`: the block runs only when this comparison is `Equal`, so a tie-breaker costs nothing once the order is already decided. Prefer it whenever the tie-breaker is more than a field read.

entries.name: Console
entries.summary:
ANSI terminal styling: colors, text attributes, and cursor control.

Every constant here becomes an empty string when Kex is started with `--no-colors`, or when output is not going to a terminal. You can splice them into a string unconditionally.

`colorize` is usually what you want, since it applies the reset for you.

entries.name: RESET
entries.summary: Clears every active style. Ends a styled run started with a color or attribute constant; `colorize` appends it for you.

entries.name: BOLD
entries.summary: Renders following text in bold.

entries.name: DIM
entries.summary: Renders following text dimmed. Useful for secondary detail that should not compete with the main output.

entries.name: ITALIC
entries.summary: Renders following text in italics, where the terminal supports it.

entries.name: UNDERLINE
entries.summary: Underlines following text.

entries.name: BLINK
entries.summary: Makes following text blink, where the terminal supports it. Most do not, and most users would rather they did not.

entries.name: REVERSE
entries.summary: Swaps the foreground and background colors of following text.

entries.name: HIDDEN
entries.summary: Hides following text: it occupies space but is not drawn.

entries.name: STRIKETHROUGH
entries.summary: Strikes through following text.

entries.name: RED
entries.summary: Red. Conventionally: errors and failures.

entries.name: GREEN
entries.summary: Green. Conventionally: success.

entries.name: YELLOW
entries.summary: Yellow. Conventionally: warnings.

entries.name: BLUE
entries.summary: Blue. Useful for informational labels and links.

entries.name: MAGENTA
entries.summary: Magenta. Useful for highlighting a category distinct from status colors.

entries.name: CYAN
entries.summary: Cyan. Useful for identifiers, paths, and other values inside prose.

entries.name: WHITE
entries.summary: White. Useful for primary text on a dark terminal.

entries.name: GRAY
entries.summary: Gray. Conventionally: de-emphasised detail, like `DIM` but as a color.

entries.name: PURPLE
entries.summary: Purple. An alternative accent when magenta is already in use.

entries.name: CLEAR
entries.summary:
Erases the screen and moves the cursor to the top-left corner.

Use it to start a fresh frame. When you are redrawing repeatedly, `HOME` gives a smoother result: see below.

entries.name: HOME
entries.summary:
Moves the cursor to the top-left corner without erasing anything.

A redraw that starts here paints over the previous frame, so there is no blank flash between frames the way `CLEAR` produces.

entries.name: CLEARLINE
entries.summary:
Erases the current line and returns the cursor to its start.

This is how to write a progress line in place rather than one line per update.

entries.name: colorize
entries.summary:
Wraps `text` in `color` and appends a reset, so the style ends where the text does.

Preferred over splicing the constants by hand: it cannot leak a style into the rest of the line, and it still produces plain text when color is off.

entries.name: enabled?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when terminal styling is on for this process.

It is `false` under `--no-colors` and when output is redirected. You rarely need to check it (the constants already collapse to `""`) but it is the right test when the alternative is a different layout rather than a different color.

entries.name: Digest
entries.summary:
Cryptographic content digests.

Digests are returned as lowercase hex strings, so a Kex program never has to handle backend-specific binary values: they compare with `==`, print directly, and go into a map key unchanged.

```kex
Digest.sha256("hello")
# => "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824"
```

SHA-256 is a content fingerprint: use it to tell whether two things are the same, to key a cache, or to check that a download arrived intact. It is not a password hash: a purpose-built password KDF is what that needs.

entries.name: sha256
entries.summary: Returns the SHA-256 digest of `content`, as a 64-character lowercase hex string.

entries.name: fileSha256
entries.summary:
Returns the SHA-256 digest of the file at `path`, or `None` when the file cannot be read.

Reads the file for you, so a large file does not have to be pulled into a `String` first.

entries.name: Dimensions
entries.summary:
Dimension algebra, implemented with ordinary Kex maps and integers.

A base dimension is identified by the type of a marker value. Reuse that marker type to share a dimension across modules. Its display name and the marker's field values do not participate in dimensional arithmetic.

Multiplication adds exponents, division subtracts them, and integer powers multiply them. Zero exponents are removed so cancellation is structural.

entries.name: Dimension
entries.summary:
A normalized map from base identities to integer exponents.

Construct dimensions with `Dimensions.base` and compose them with arithmetic. If importing a map, use `Dimensions.fromPowers` to remove zero exponents. This runtime representation does not itself provide static measure typing.

entries.name: one
entries.summary: The dimension with no remaining base factors.

entries.name: base
entries.summary: Defines a base dimension using the nominal type of a marker value.

entries.name: fromPowers
entries.summary: Normalizes a map of base identities and powers.

entries.name: dimensionless?
entries.summary: Whether every base factor has cancelled.

entries.name: exponentOf
entries.summary: The exponent of the supplied marker's dimension, or zero if absent.
Composes dimensions by adding their base exponents.
Composes dimensions by subtracting the denominator's exponents.
Raises a dimension to an integer power, including zero and negatives.

entries.name: Foldable
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> T -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Traversal operations that every foldable collection gets for free.

A type becomes `Foldable` by implementing one method, `reduce`; the rest: `each`, `all?`, `any?`, `find`, `count`: are derived from it. `List`, `String`, `Map`, `Range` and both flavours of `Set` all implement it, so these methods read the same whatever you point them at.

```kex
[1, 2, 3].all? { |n| n > 0 }        # => true
"hello".any?(~digit?)               # => false
{ a: 1, b: 2 }.count { |k, v| v > 1 }   # => 1
```

Blocks are applied via Kex.Intrinsic.Fun.applyItem, which auto-splats a pair item into a two-argument block. That is what lets a `Map` traversal be written `{ |key, value| ... }` even though the fold hands over one tuple.

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> T -> A)) -> A
entries.summary: Folds the collection from the left. The one operation a `Foldable` type must define; everything else here is written in terms of it.

entries.name: each
entries.summary:
Calls `f` with each item, for its side effects.

The loop of last resort, when what you want is a new collection rather than an effect, `map` or `filter` says so more clearly.

entries.name: eachIndexed
entries.summary:
Calls `f` with each item and its 0-based position, for its side effects.

The index is the LAST block parameter, so a `Map` entry can be taken either whole (`|entry, i|`) or spread (`|k, v, i|`).

entries.name: all?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when every item satisfies `pred`. An empty collection answers `true`.

entries.name: any?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when at least one item satisfies `pred`. An empty collection answers `false`.

entries.name: find
entries.summary: Returns the first item satisfying `pred`, or `None` when nothing does.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns how many items satisfy `pred`.

entries.name: Enumerable
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> T -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Collection-producing operations that every foldable collection gets for free.

Like `Foldable`, a type joins by implementing `reduce` alone. The defaults here answer with a list, because the block may return anything at all; a type that can do better overrides them: `Map.filter` gives back a map, `Set.map` gives back a set, `String.filter` gives back a string.

```kex
[1, 2, 3].map { |n| n * 2 }              # => [2, 4, 6]
"a1b2".filter(~digit?)                   # => "12"
{ a: 1, b: 2 }.filter { |k, v| v > 1 }   # => { :b: 2 }
```

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> T -> A)) -> A
entries.summary: Folds the collection from the left. The one operation an `Enumerable` type must define.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each item and collects the results into a list.

The single most useful method here: it describes what each item becomes, and leaves the walking of the collection implied.

entries.name: mapIndexed
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each item and its 0-based position, and collects the results into a list.

The index is the LAST block parameter: see `eachIndexed`.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary: Returns the items for which `pred` answers `true`.

entries.name: flatMap
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each item, expecting a list back, and concatenates the results into one flat list.

Use it when each item expands into zero or more results: `map` would give you a list of lists.

entries.name: collect
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each item, expecting an `Optional` back, and returns the values that were present: unwrapped.

This is filter and map fused into one pass, which is what you want whenever the test and the transformation are the same operation. Parsing is the classic case: an item either yields a value or it does not.

entries.name: ENV
entries.summary:
The process environment, as an immutable `Map<String, String>` snapshot taken at startup.

`ENV` supports the whole `Map` API: `get`, `has?`, `keys`, `values`, `count`, `each`, `entries`, so reading a variable looks like any other map lookup:

```kex
ENV.get("HOME")                  # => Just("/home/ada")
ENV.get("LOG_LEVEL", "info")     # => "info" when unset
ENV.has?("PATH")                 # => true
```

The snapshot itself is immutable, but the global `ENV` namespace is an ambient input: the same call can answer differently between runs without anything appearing in a function's arguments. That is why reading it is `foul`.

When you would rather the dependency be visible, take it as a parameter: `main` receives the same snapshot as its second argument, and reading a parameter is pure:

```kex
main(args, env) do
  let level = env.get("LOG_LEVEL", "info")
  IO.printLine("log level: ${level}")
end
```

entries.name: get
entries.summary: Returns the value of the environment variable `key`, or `None` when it is not set.

entries.name: has?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `key` is set, whatever its value.

Distinguishes an unset variable from one set to the empty string, which a `get` with a default cannot.

entries.name: keys
entries.summary: Returns every variable name in the environment.

entries.name: values
entries.summary: Returns every variable value in the environment.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns how many variables the environment has.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each variable's name and value.

entries.name: entries
entries.summary:
Returns the environment as a list of `(name, value)` pairs.

The bridge to the `List` operations, sorting, grouping, taking a slice.

entries.name: set
entries.summary:
Sets an environment variable for this process and every child it starts.

`ENV` is a snapshot, and the write rebuilds it: a later `ENV.get` answers what was set, not what the process started with.

This is how a program decides what a child sees. `Kex.AST`, for instance, shells out to the compiler named by `$KEX`, so a tool that knows which compiler it means says so here rather than hoping `PATH` agrees.

Sets a variable for THIS process and every child it starts. `ENV` is a snapshot, so it is rebuilt by the write: a later `ENV.get` answers what was set, not what the process started with.

This is how a program decides what a child sees: `Kex.AST` shells out to the compiler named by `$KEX`, so a tool that knows which compiler it means says so here rather than hoping PATH agrees.

entries.name: unset
entries.summary: Removes an environment variable from this process and its children.

entries.name: Errorable
entries.summary:
`Errorable`: the trait for values that describe a failure.

Implemented by error types that carry a human-readable message, so a generic handler can display or log any error without knowing its concrete type or its structured fields.

```kex
foul report(e: Errorable) -> Void do
  IO.printError("error: ${e.message}")
end
```

entries.name: message
entries.summary:
A human-readable description of what went wrong.

Written for a person reading output, not for a program to match on: branch on the error's own type or fields for that.

entries.name: ParseError
entries.summary:
A parse failure, with everything needed to report it or to carry on from it.

Answered by `Integer.parse`, `Float.parse` and `Number.parse` when the input is not what they expected. Reach for those over `to(Integer)` exactly when this detail matters: `to` answers a plain `None`.

```kex
Integer.parse("12x")
# => Error(ParseError { input: "12x", position: 2, value: 12,
#                       message: "trailing characters after integer",
#                       rest: "x" })
```

The `position` and `rest` are what make a hand-written scanner possible: the error says exactly where it stopped and what was left.

entries.name: Evaluator
signatures: run(source: String, opts: EvaluatorOptions) -> Result<Any, String>
runExpression(source: String, opts: EvaluatorOptions) -> Result<Any, String>
entries.summary:
Running Kex source code at run time, in a sandbox.

Each call builds a fresh, isolated evaluator: the caller's environment is never shared, and the evaluated code sees only what `EvaluatorOptions` allows. Step and depth limits make a runaway program stop rather than hang.

```kex
Evaluator.runExpression("1 + 2")           # => Ok(3)
Evaluator.runExpression("[3,1,2].sort")    # => Ok([1, 2, 3])
```

This is for evaluating expressions your program was given: a formula in a config file, a filter typed by a user. Every result is a `Result`, so a syntax error or a rejected call is a value you handle.

entries.name: run
signatures: run(source: String, opts: EvaluatorOptions) -> Result<Any, String>
entries.summary:
Evaluates a whole Kex program and returns its result.

The source may declare functions, records and a `main`, exactly as a file would. Anything that goes wrong: a parse error, a call the sandbox does not allow, running past the step limit: comes back as `Error` with a message.

entries.name: runExpression
signatures: runExpression(source: String, opts: EvaluatorOptions) -> Result<Any, String>
entries.summary:
Evaluates a single Kex expression and returns its value.

The form to reach for when the input is a formula rather than a program: there is no `main` to write and no declarations to skip past.

entries.name: EvaluatorOptions
entries.summary:
What an evaluated program is allowed to reach, and how long it may run.

The defaults are already conservative: pure computation over the common data types, no filesystem, no network, no processes. Narrow `allow` further, or lower the limits, when the source is less trusted still.

entries.name: Feed
entries.summary:
A one-shot sequence over a source that can only be read once.

A feed is what `Stream` is not: reading it CONSUMES it. Where a stream remembers its elements so it can be walked again, a feed keeps nothing, and that is the point: it is how to walk a file, a socket or a device larger than memory, which a stream cannot do while anything still holds its start.

```kex
foul lines = FS.File.feed("huge.log").or(Feed.empty)
lines.each { |line| IO.printLine(line) if line.contains?("ERROR") }
```

`map`, `filter` and `drop` answer a feed over the SAME cursor rather than a second cursor over the same source, so a pipeline is one pass:

```kex
FS.File.feed("app.log").or(Feed.empty)
  .filter { |line| line.contains?("ERROR") }
  .take(10)
```

Taking twice answers two different windows: the first ten, then the ten after them. That is the whole difference from `Stream`, where taking twice answers the same ten. When you want the stream behaviour on a small source, `toStream` asks for it explicitly, at the cost of holding what it reads.

entries.name: Feed
entries.summary: Constructors for `Feed`.

entries.name: empty
entries.summary:
A feed with nothing in it, already spent.

Mostly the `or` half of a failed open: `FS.File.feed(path).or(Feed.empty)` reads nothing rather than stopping the program.

entries.name: Elements
entries.summary:
A feed over a list that is already in hand.

The elements are there, so nothing is saved by feeding them: this is for standing in for a real source, in a test, with something that consumes the way the real one does.

entries.name: Feed<A>
entries.summary:
Every method below is `let`, not `foul`, though reading a feed plainly is an effect. Two reasons, one principled and one practical.

The effect is already tracked where it enters: a feed over anything outside the program comes from `FS.File.feed` or `handle.feed`, both foul, so a pure function cannot obtain one. What `Feed.Elements` and `Stream.toFeed` build from data in hand mutates only a cursor the caller just made.

And a foul method takes the hidden capability context, which puts it one BEAM arity above the pure `take`/`map`/`filter` every other receiver has. A feed usually arrives with no static type: `FS.File.feed(p).or(Feed.empty)`, or a `Just(f) =>` binding, and such a call has to go through the runtime dispatcher, which is built per arity and so could never reach a method one arity up. Marking these foul made every dynamically-typed feed call fail with "Undefined method: take for Tuple".

entries.name: pull
entries.summary:
Answers the next element and consumes it, or `None` once the source is spent.

NOT named `next`: that is the loop-continue keyword, and the lexer reads it as one even after a dot, so a call to it silently swallows the rest of the enclosing block.

entries.name: spent?
entries.summary:
Whether the source has run out.

`false` does not promise another element: only that the feed has not been told otherwise yet. The source is asked, and may end, on the next read.

entries.name: take
entries.summary:
Returns the next `n` elements as a list, consuming them.

Answers fewer than `n` when the source ends first, and `[]` once it is spent. Unlike `Stream.take`, calling it twice walks forward.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary:
Discards the next `n` elements and answers the feed.

There is only ever one cursor, so this hands back the same feed rather than a second one positioned differently.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Returns a feed with `f` applied to each element.

`f` runs as elements are read, and only for those that are. The result draws from the same cursor, so reading it consumes the receiver too.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary:
Returns a feed of only the elements `pred` accepts.

Reading one element of the result may consume many of the receiver's.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Applies `f` to every remaining element, draining the feed.

entries.name: collect
entries.summary:
Drains the feed into a list.

This is the operation that gives up constant space, which is why it is named rather than implicit: on a source too large to hold, use `each`.

entries.name: toStream
entries.summary:
Returns a `Stream` drawn from the feed.

The stream remembers what it reads, so it can be walked again: at the cost of holding every element forced through it. Worth it for a source small enough to replay; the opposite of what a feed is for otherwise.

entries.name: ReadError
entries.summary:
Why a read failed.

`ReadFailed` means the source refused the read. `InvalidUtf8` means bytes were read but are not valid UTF-8, and carries the byte offset of the first malformed sequence, relative to that one operation. A failed read consumes the bytes it attempted to read and never substitutes U+FFFD: use `readBytes` to recover the payload verbatim.

entries.name: Readable
entries.summary:
`Readable`: a source that yields text.

Named so that anything can be one, not just a file: the vocabulary `FileHandle<CanRead, W>` already carried was an abstraction without a name, so nothing else could implement it and `IO` did not go through it (kexhq/kex#139). `IO.in` is a `Readable`; so is any handle opened for reading.

```kex
foul firstLine(source: Readable) -> String do
  source.getLine.or("(empty)")
end

firstLine(IO.in)
firstLine(FS.File.open("notes.txt", Read).try)
```

entries.name: getLine
entries.summary: Reads the next line, without its newline.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Reads a single character, as a one-character `String`.

Reads one complete Unicode scalar, not one byte.

entries.name: readLine
entries.summary: Reads the next line, without its newline. The same as `getLine`.

entries.name: read
entries.summary:
Reads everything remaining, as one `String`.

Draining an exhausted source answers `Ok("")`.

entries.name: readBytes
entries.summary:
Reads everything remaining as raw bytes, without decoding it as text.

The byte counterpart of `read`: it never validates UTF-8, so it recovers the payload of a source that is not text, or one `read` has just rejected. Draining an exhausted source answers `Ok(Binary.fromBytes([]))`.

entries.name: eof?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the source has reached its end.

entries.name: atEnd?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the source has reached its end. The same as `eof?`.

entries.name: Writable
entries.summary:
`Writable`: a sink that accepts text.

The payoff of naming it is that a sink becomes a VALUE a library can accept, rather than a global switch it can only sit underneath: output from one library can go to a buffer while another's goes to the terminal (kexhq/kex#139).

```kex
foul report(out: Writable, lines: [String]) -> Void do
  lines.each { |line| out.printLine(line) }
end

report(IO.out, results)
report(IO.error, warnings)
report(FS.File.open("report.txt", Write).try, results)
```

Two deliberate choices, both settled in kexhq/kex#139:

- The argument is `Showable`, not `String`. `IO.printLine` always took a   `Showable` while the handle methods took a `String`; the wider one is   right, and it is what makes `IO.printLine(x)` and `IO.out.printLine(x)`   the same call. - The result is `Void`, not `Bool`. A boolean nobody checks is not an error   channel, and `Result<Void, IOError>` on every print is miserable to use.   Erlang's answer is the one taken here: the call says `ok`, and failure   belongs to the device rather than to the call site.

entries.name: printLine
entries.summary: Writes `content` followed by a newline.

entries.name: print
entries.summary: Writes `content` with no trailing newline.

entries.name: writeLine
entries.summary: Writes `content` followed by a newline. The same as `printLine`.

entries.name: write
entries.summary: Writes `content` with no trailing newline. The same as `print`.

entries.name: writeBytes
entries.summary:
Writes `content` as raw bytes, with no trailing newline.

The byte counterpart of `write`: the payload goes to the sink exactly as given. It never renders the value, so a `Binary` reaches the sink as its bytes rather than as the `#Binary<N bytes>` that `Showable` would print.

entries.name: FileHandle
entries.summary:
An open file, obtained from `FS.File.open`.

The two type parameters record what the handle is allowed to do: `R` is `CanRead` or `CannotRead`, `W` is `CanWrite` or `CannotWrite`. `FS.File.open` picks them from the mode you pass, so calling `write` on a handle opened `Read` is a compile error rather than a run-time failure.

```kex
using FS

main do
  match FS.File.open("notes.txt", Read) do
    Ok(handle) => do
      IO.printLine(handle.read.or(""))
      handle.close
    end
    Error(e) => IO.printError("cannot open: ${e}")
  end
end
```

Reach for a handle when you want to walk a large file a line at a time, or make many small writes. When a file fits comfortably in memory, `FS.File.read` and `FS.File.write` are shorter and need no closing. To be rid of the closing entirely, pass `FS.File.open` a block.

The handle methods are `foul`: obtaining a handle is not an effect, but reading or writing through one is, so a function that does so is `foul` no matter where the handle came from. Injection makes a thing substitutable, not pure.

entries.name: getLine
entries.summary:
Reads the next line from the handle, without its newline.

Answers `None` at end of file, which is what makes it usable as a loop condition. The same operation as `readLine`, under the name `IO.getLine` uses.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Reads a single character from the handle, as a one-character `String`.

Answers `None` at end of file.

entries.name: readLine
entries.summary: Reads the next line from the handle, without its newline. The same as `getLine`, named for reading from a file rather than from a console.

entries.name: read
entries.summary:
Reads everything remaining in the file and returns it as one `String`.

Reads from the current position, so calling it after a `readLine` gives the rest of the file rather than the whole of it.

entries.name: readBytes
entries.summary:
Reads all remaining bytes from the handle without decoding them.

Unlike `read`, this accepts arbitrary binary data and cannot fail because the input is not valid UTF-8. It starts at the handle's current position.

entries.name: eof?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the handle has reached the end of the file.

entries.name: atEnd?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the handle has reached the end of the file. The same as `eof?`, spelled out.

entries.name: feed
entries.summary:
Returns the handle's remaining lines as a lazy `Feed`.

Lines are read on demand off the handle's own position, so this is how to look at the start of a very large file, or process one without holding it all in memory. The feed shares the handle's cursor: interleaving `readLine` with it advances one position through one open file.

The feed ends at the last line, so taking more lines than the file has answers just the lines there are.

NOT part of `Readable`: a feed is neither pure nor reusable, so requiring it of every `Readable` would put a foul, one-shot operation on types that have no such cursor to offer. It stays a FileHandle method.

entries.name: writeBytes
entries.summary: Writes `content` verbatim, without text encoding or a trailing newline.

entries.name: printLine
entries.summary: Writes `content` followed by a newline.

entries.name: print
entries.summary: Writes `content` with no trailing newline.

entries.name: writeLine
entries.summary: Writes `content` followed by a newline. The same as `printLine`, named for writing to a file rather than to a console.

entries.name: write
entries.summary: Writes `content` with no trailing newline. The same as `print`.

entries.name: close
entries.summary:
Closes the handle, flushing anything still buffered.

Close every handle you open. A written file is not guaranteed to be complete on disk until its handle is closed. Passing `FS.File.open` a block closes the handle for you.

entries.name: seek
entries.summary: Moves the handle's cursor to an absolute byte offset from the start of the file. Read and write share one cursor, so this repositions both — a `readLine` right after `seek(0)` starts over from the top, and a `write` right after does too, overwriting from that point.

entries.name: reset
entries.summary: Moves the handle's cursor back to the start of the file — the same as `seek(0)`, for the common case of re-reading a handle from the top.

entries.name: FS
signatures: open(path: FilePath, mode: Read) -> Result<FileHandle<CanRead, CannotWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Write) -> Result<FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Append) -> Result<FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: ReadWrite) -> Result<FileHandle<CanRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Read) -> (FileHandle<CanRead, CannotWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Write) -> (FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Append) -> (FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: ReadWrite) -> (FileHandle<CanRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
join(a: FilePath, b: FilePath) -> FilePath -> String
entries.summary:
The filesystem: reading and writing files, walking directories, and manipulating paths.

`FS` is not in the prelude: start with `using FS`.

```kex
using FS

main do
  match FS.File.read("config.txt") do
    Just(text) => IO.printLine(text.lines.count)
    None       => IO.printError("config.txt is missing")
  end
end
```

It is organised in three parts:

```kex
FS.File        reading, writing, copying and deleting files
FS.Directory   creating, listing and removing directories
FS.Path        pure path arithmetic, with no filesystem access at all
```

The first two are capabilities: everything in them touches the real filesystem, so they can only be called from `foul` code, and a test can replace the whole of `FS.File` for a lexical region rather than mutating global state. `FS.Path` is ordinary pure code.

Most read operations answer with an `Optional` and most write operations with a `Bool`, so a missing file or a failed write is an ordinary value you handle rather than an exception you catch.

entries.name: FilePath
entries.summary: A filesystem path. An alias for `String`, so every `String` method applies to one; `FS.Path` adds the path-aware operations.

entries.name: FileModes
entries.summary: How a file should be opened: `Read` to read it, `Write` to replace it, `Append` to add to its end, `ReadWrite` for both. The mode chosen decides what type the resulting `FileHandle` has, and therefore which operations the compiler will let you call on it.

entries.name: ReadPermission
entries.summary: Whether a `FileHandle` may be read from. Part of the handle's type rather than a runtime flag, so reading from a write-only handle is a compile error.

entries.name: WritePermission
entries.summary: Whether a `FileHandle` may be written to. Part of the handle's type, so writing to a read-only handle is a compile error.

entries.name: FileError
entries.summary:
A file operation that failed, carrying the path it failed on.

`OpenFailed` and `ReadFailed` mean the filesystem refused the operation. `InvalidUtf8` means the bytes were read but are not valid UTF-8, and carries the byte offset of the first malformed sequence.

entries.name: FS.File
signatures: open(path: FilePath, mode: Read) -> Result<FileHandle<CanRead, CannotWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Write) -> Result<FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Append) -> Result<FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: ReadWrite) -> Result<FileHandle<CanRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Read) -> (FileHandle<CanRead, CannotWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Write) -> (FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Append) -> (FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: ReadWrite) -> (FileHandle<CanRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
entries.summary:
Reading and writing files.

A capability: every member reaches the real filesystem, so a test can replace the whole thing for a lexical region with `with FS.File = ...` instead of mutating global mock state (kexhq/kex#143). The boundary is here rather than on `FS`, because `FS.Path` below is pure string work with no implementation to substitute.

entries.name: open
signatures: open(path: FilePath, mode: Read) -> Result<FileHandle<CanRead, CannotWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Write) -> Result<FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Append) -> Result<FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: ReadWrite) -> Result<FileHandle<CanRead, CanWrite>, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Read) -> (FileHandle<CanRead, CannotWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Write) -> (FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: Append) -> (FileHandle<CannotRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
open(path: FilePath, mode: ReadWrite) -> (FileHandle<CanRead, CanWrite> -> A) -> Result<A, FileError>
entries.summary:
Opens `path` and returns a `FileHandle` for it.

The mode decides the handle's type, and the type decides what you may do with it: a handle opened `Read` has no `write`, a handle opened `Write` has no `read`. That is checked at compile time, not at run time.

Use the whole-file `read` and `write` below when a file fits in memory and you have no reason to hold it open; reach for a handle when you want to stream through a large file or make many small writes.

Close the handle when you are done with it.

entries.name: read
entries.summary:
Reads the whole file and decodes it as UTF-8 text.

Answers `Error(ReadFailed(path))` when the file does not exist or cannot be read, and `Error(InvalidUtf8(path, offset))` when the bytes are not valid UTF-8, so a missing or non-text file is something you handle rather than something that stops the program. Reach for `FS.File.readBytes` when the contents are not text.

entries.name: readBytes
entries.summary:
Reads the whole file as raw bytes, without decoding it as text.

The byte counterpart of `FS.File.read`: it never validates UTF-8, so it round trips images, archives, and any other non-text payload losslessly. Answers `Error(ReadFailed(path))` when the file cannot be read.

entries.name: writeBytes
entries.summary:
Writes `content` to `path` as raw bytes, replacing whatever was there.

The byte counterpart of `FS.File.write`: the payload lands on disk exactly as given, with no encoding step. Answers `false` when the write fails.

entries.name: write
entries.summary:
Writes `content` to `path`, replacing whatever was there.

Creates the file if it does not exist. The containing directory must already exist: see `FS.Directory.create`. Answers `false` when the write fails.

entries.name: append
entries.summary:
Adds `content` to the end of `path`, keeping what is already there.

Creates the file if it does not exist, so it is safe to append to a log that has not been started yet.

entries.name: exists?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when something exists at `path`: a file, a directory, or anything else. Use `file?` or `directory?` when the kind matters.

entries.name: file?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when `path` exists and is a regular file: not a directory.

entries.name: directory?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when `path` exists and is a directory.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary:
Deletes the file at `path`.

Answers `false` when the file does not exist or cannot be removed. Use `FS.Directory.delete` for a directory.

entries.name: copy
entries.summary: Copies the file at `src` to `dst`, replacing `dst` if it exists.

entries.name: rename
entries.summary: Renames (or moves) the file at `src` to `dst`.

entries.name: readLines
entries.summary:
Reads the file and returns its lines, without their newlines.

Answers `None` when the file cannot be read. A trailing newline does not produce a final empty line, so the count is the number of lines you would see in an editor.

NOT `lines`: FilePath is an alias for String, so a receiver function named `lines` here is indistinguishable from String's own `lines` at every call site, and merely saying `using FS` made `text.lines` ambiguous. `readLines` also says what it does: it reads the file.

entries.name: feed
entries.summary:
Returns a lazy `Feed` of the file's lines, or `None` when it cannot be read.

Unlike `readLines`, the file is read a line at a time off a handle held open for the feed's lifetime, so this is the way to walk a file too large to hold in memory: nothing but the current line is retained.

A `Feed` rather than a `Stream` because that is what a file honestly is: reading consumes, and there is no rewinding. Taking twice walks forward rather than answering the same lines again. On a file small enough to replay, `toStream` buys that back.

The feed ends at the last line, so asking for more lines than the file has answers just the lines there are: unlike `Stream.Sequence`, which is deliberately infinite.

```kex
FS.File.feed("two-lines.txt").map { |lines| lines.take(5) }.or([])
# => ["one", "two"]
```

entries.name: size
entries.summary:
Returns the file's size in bytes, or `None` when it cannot be read.

Bytes, not characters: a file of non-ASCII text has more bytes than it has characters.

entries.name: absolute
entries.summary:
Resolves `path` against the process's current directory and returns the absolute form, or `None` when it cannot be resolved.

This is the one path operation that is not in `FS.Path`, because it is not lexical: it asks the process where it is.

Path manipulation lives in FS.Path: `basename`, `dirname`, `extension` and `join` used to be here too, but a name cannot sit in both modules: FilePath IS String, so two same-named receiver functions on it are indistinguishable at every call site. `absolute` stays because it is not lexical: it asks the process where it is.

entries.name: canonical
entries.summary:
The canonical form of `path`: absolute, with every `.`, `..` and symlink resolved, like `realpath(3)`.

Unlike `absolute` this reads the filesystem, so a path that does not exist (or a symlink loop) is an error. Use it to keep reads and writes inside a directory: compare the real path's prefix, and neither `../` nor a symlink can escape.

entries.name: symlink?
entries.summary: Whether `path` is itself a symlink, without following it. A dangling link is still a symlink.

entries.name: FS.Path
signatures: join(a: FilePath, b: FilePath) -> FilePath -> String
entries.summary:
Path arithmetic: joining, splitting, normalising and comparing paths.

Everything here is pure string manipulation with no filesystem access, so the answer is the same whether or not the path exists, which also means these functions can be called from ordinary pure code, unlike `FS.File`. POSIX separators only for now.

```kex
FS.Path.join("src", "main.kex")            # => "src/main.kex"
FS.Path.extension("src/main.kex")          # => ".kex"
FS.Path.withExtension("src/main.kex", "beam")   # => "src/main.beam"
```

entries.name: separator
entries.summary: The path separator, `"/"`.

entries.name: join
signatures: join(a: FilePath, b: FilePath) -> FilePath -> String
entries.summary:
Joins two path parts with a single separator and normalises the result.

Repeated separators collapse, so `join("a/", "/b")` is `"a/b"` and not `"a//b"`. An absolute second part does NOT restart the path, the way Ruby's `Pathname#join` would: use that part on its own if that is what you mean.

entries.name: joinAll
entries.summary:
Joins any number of path parts, skipping empty ones, and normalises the result. An empty list gives `"."`.

The list form is `joinAll`, not another `join` overload: a list receiver already has `List.join`, and a second one-argument `join` on the same receiver would be indistinguishable from it.

entries.name: normalize
entries.summary:
Resolves `.` and `..` in a path, lexically.

Because it is lexical it never follows a symlink and never touches the disk. A leading `..` in a RELATIVE path is kept: there is no way to know what it escapes to, while one in an absolute path is dropped, since `/` has no parent.

entries.name: segments
entries.summary: Returns the non-empty parts of the normalised path. The root `/` and the current directory `.` have none.

entries.name: absolute?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the path starts at the root.

entries.name: relative?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the path does not start at the root. The opposite of `absolute?`.

entries.name: dirname
entries.summary:
Returns the path's parent directory.

A child of the root has `"/"` as its parent; a bare name has `"."`, the current directory.

entries.name: basename
entries.summary:
Returns the last segment of the path: the file or directory name.

The root itself answers `"/"`, and an empty path answers `"."`.

entries.name: extension
entries.summary:
Returns the file extension, including its leading dot, or `""` when there is none.

Only the last extension counts, so `"a.tar.gz"` has `".gz"`. A leading dot is part of the NAME rather than an extension, so `".gitignore"` has none.

entries.name: stem
entries.summary:
Returns the basename with its extension removed.

A name that IS its extension (`".gitignore"`) keeps it, because it has none to drop.

entries.name: withExtension
entries.summary:
Returns the path with its extension replaced by `wanted`.

The new extension may be written with or without its leading dot; an empty one removes the extension entirely.

entries.name: relativeTo
entries.summary:
Expresses `path` relative to `base`, walking up with `..` as needed.

Purely lexical, so it answers only when both sides are anchored the same way; a relative path against an absolute base, or the reverse, comes back unchanged. A path that IS the base answers `"."`.

entries.name: FS.Directory
entries.summary:
Creating, listing and removing directories.

Like `FS.File`, everything here reaches the real filesystem and so is `foul`. Listings answer with an `Optional`, so a directory that cannot be read is a value you handle rather than an exception.

entries.name: exists?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when something exists at `path`.

entries.name: directory?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when `path` exists and is a directory.

entries.name: file?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when `path` exists and is a regular file.

entries.name: create
entries.summary: Creates the directory at `path`.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary:
Removes the directory at `path`, which must be empty.

Use `deleteAll` to remove a directory together with its contents.

entries.name: deleteAll
entries.summary:
Removes the directory at `path` and everything inside it, recursively.

This deletes data and cannot be undone: check the path before calling it, particularly when it was computed or came from user input.

entries.name: list
entries.summary:
Lists the names in `path`: both files and directories, one level deep.

The results are bare names, not paths; join them with `path` to get something you can open. Answers `None` when the directory cannot be read.

entries.name: files
entries.summary: Lists only the regular files in `path`, one level deep.

entries.name: directories
entries.summary: Lists only the subdirectories of `path`, one level deep.

entries.name: current
entries.summary: Returns the process's current working directory, as an absolute path.

entries.name: home
entries.summary: Returns the current user's home directory, or `None` when it cannot be determined.

entries.name: temporary
entries.summary:
Returns the directory this system puts temporary files in.

Total, unlike `home`: it answers `TMPDIR` when the environment sets one (`TEMP` or `TMP` on Windows) and falls back to `/tmp`, so there is always somewhere to write. The path never ends in a separator, so it composes with `FS.Path.join` directly.

The directory is shared with every other process on the machine, so pick a name unlikely to collide and delete it when you are done.

entries.name: IO
entries.summary:
Console input and output.

`IO` is a capability: every function in it touches the outside world, so it can only be called from `foul` code (or from `main`). Reading a line and printing a line are the two workhorses; `inspect` is the debugging tool that can be dropped into the middle of a chain without changing its value.

```kex
main do
  IO.print("name? ")
  let name = IO.getLine.or("world")
  IO.printLine("hello, ${name.trim}")
end
```

entries.name: printLine
entries.summary:
Writes `msg` to stdout followed by a newline.

Any `Showable` value is accepted, not just strings: numbers, lists, maps and records print through their own `show` implementation. Called with no argument it prints an empty line.

entries.name: print
entries.summary:
Writes `msg` to stdout without a trailing newline.

Use it to build a line from several pieces, or to write a prompt that the cursor should stay on.

entries.name: inspect
entries.summary:
Writes a colored, structured rendering of `val` to stderr and returns `val` unchanged.

Because it returns its argument, `inspect` can be spliced into the middle of a chain to see what is flowing through it, then removed again without touching the surrounding code. It writes to stderr, so it does not disturb a program whose stdout is piped somewhere. The type checker treats it as pure, so it is allowed inside pure functions.

Use `inspected` instead when you want the rendering as a `String` rather than written out.

entries.name: getLine
entries.summary:
Reads one line from stdin, without the trailing newline.

Returns `None` at end of input, which is what makes it usable as a loop condition: the `None` is the end of the stream, not an error.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Reads a single character from stdin.

Returns `None` at end of input. Note that the result is a one-character `String`, not a `Char`.

entries.name: printError
entries.summary:
Writes `msg` to stderr followed by a newline.

Diagnostics belong on stderr so that a program's real output can be piped or redirected on its own. Unlike a raised error, this only prints: it does not stop the program.

entries.name: warn
entries.summary: Writes `msg` to stderr. Identical to `printError`, named for the case where the message is a warning rather than a failure.

entries.name: warning
entries.summary: Writes `msg` to stderr. The long spelling of `warn`.

entries.name: out
entries.summary:
The three standard streams, as ordinary handle VALUES.

`IO.printLine(x)` and `IO.out.printLine(x)` are the same call: the convenience spelling stays, and the handle behind it is now something a program can name, pass and substitute. That is what `Mock.IO` cannot do: it is one global switch, so output from one library cannot go to a buffer while another's goes to the terminal, and a library cannot ACCEPT a sink (kexhq/kex#139).

Typestate says what each one permits: writing to `IO.in`, or reading from `IO.out`, is a compile error, exactly as it is for a file opened `Read`.

These three are PURE, so they are not part of the capability interface a stand-in must implement: naming a device performs no effect, writing THROUGH it does, and the handle methods are the `foul` ones. That also draws the seam between the two ways to redirect output: `with IO = ...` replaces the CALLS, so it does not touch a handle obtained here, while `Mock.IO` replaces the DEVICE (a group leader, kexhq/kex#141) and so captures `IO.out.printLine(x)` and `IO.printLine(x)` alike.

entries.name: error
entries.summary: Standard error, as a handle. The sink `IO.printError` and `IO.warn` write to, reachable as a value.

entries.name: in
entries.summary: Standard input, as a handle. The source `IO.getLine` and `IO.get` read from, reachable as a value.

entries.name: JSON
signatures: parse(text: String, options: {Atom: Bool}) -> Result<Any, Error>

entries.name: Error
entries.summary:
Why a document could not be parsed. Every variant carries the position in the input where the parser stopped, so a caller can point at the problem.

```kex
JSON.parse("[1, 2")    # => Error(UnexpectedEnd(5))
JSON.parse("// c\n1")  # => Error(UnexpectedCharacter("/", 0))
```

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(text: String, options: {Atom: Bool}) -> Result<Any, Error>
entries.summary:
Parses a JSON document, strictly.

The whole text must be one JSON value with nothing after it: trailing input is `TrailingInput`, not a silently ignored tail. Objects come back as maps with atom keys, arrays as lists, `null` as `None`.

entries.name: stringify
entries.summary:
Renders a Kex value as strict JSON text.

Maps become objects, lists become arrays, `None` becomes `null`, and strings are escaped. A map written with atom keys (the usual Kex spelling) renders with those names as strings, so `{ name: "Ada" }` becomes `{"name":"Ada"}`. Object keys come out in canonical key order.

Anything the encoder does not recognise renders as `null` rather than failing, so this never raises.

entries.name: Inspectable
entries.summary:
Types that can be rendered structurally, for a person reading output.

The rendering shows the value's STRUCTURE: quotes on strings, `Just(...)` around an optional, which is what makes it right for debugging and wrong for user-facing text. `Showable` is the other half of that pair.

Every type is inspectable through a structural fallback, so `inspected` and `IO.inspect` work on anything; a type that wants a different rendering overrides `inspectValue`.

```kex
[1, 2].inspected       # => "[1, 2]"
Just("hi").inspected   # => "Just(\"hi\")"
```

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary:
Renders the value structurally, with ANSI colors when `colors` is true.

`inspected` and `IO.inspect` call this for you, passing the console's own color setting: call it directly only when you need to force one.

entries.name: Showable
entries.summary:
Types that have a concise, user-facing text representation.

`Showable` is used by interpolation, printing, and `to(String)`. Its output should describe the value itself rather than its implementation structure: a string is shown without quotes, `Just(x)` is shown as `x`, and `None` is shown as an empty string. Use `Inspectable` when debugging structure matters.

```kex
"hello".showValue          # => "hello"
Just("hello").showValue    # => "hello"
None.showValue             # => ""
```

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary:
Returns the value's user-facing text representation.

Implement this for domain types whose useful presentation differs from their structural rendering. Keep the result free of ANSI styling so it is safe in files, logs, and interpolation as well as on a terminal.

entries.name: Inspectable
entries.summary: Structural fallback: the runtime only decomposes the value; implementation selection and overrides remain ordinary Kex trait dispatch.

entries.name: Showable
entries.summary: Current non-colored presentation for the primitive and standard compound types registered as Showable. Domain types can replace this with what their users care about (Time, Date, and DateTime do so in time.kex).

entries.name: Result<X, E>
entries.summary:
The same for Result, with one deliberate asymmetry: SHOWING a result shows what it carries, so `Ok(42)` reads as `42` rather than leaking the wrapper into text, but an `Error` keeps its marker. Dropping it made a failure and a success print identically, and unlike `None` (which shows as "", visibly not a value) there would be nothing left to tell them apart.

The marker is spelled `Error(...)`, matching how the same value renders as an ELEMENT of a collection: `[1, Error(Bad(no))]`. Elements render structurally rather than through showValue (as in Ruby, where `nil.to_s` is "" but `[nil].to_s` is "[nil]"), so this is the one spelling that reads the same at both levels.

What functions RETURN is unchanged: `Integer.parse` still answers with a Result, `IO.inspect` still shows `Ok(42)`, and both arms are still matchable.

entries.name: Kex
entries.summary:
The running toolchain, which backend, which version, which features.

```kex
Kex.BACKEND                  # => Interpreter
Kex.BACKEND.compiled?        # => false
Kex.VERSION.release          # => "0.4.0"
Kex.Feature.has?(Kex.FileSystem)   # => true
```

entries.name: Backend
entries.summary: Which backend is executing the program: the tree-walking `Interpreter`, or the `Beam` virtual machine.

entries.name: interpreted?
entries.summary: Whether this is the tree-walking interpreter.

entries.name: compiled?
entries.summary: Whether this backend runs compiled code: today, the BEAM.

entries.name: beam?
entries.summary: Whether this is the BEAM virtual machine. Processes, the web server and clustering need it.

entries.name: Feature
entries.summary:
An optional capability a build may or may not include. Ask about one with `Kex.Feature.has?` before relying on it.

`FileSystem`: the program can read and write the host's files (`FS`). `ExternalPrograms`: it can run other programs (`Process.run`, `Process.stream`), which the browser build cannot.

Kex's own processes (`spawn`, `receive`) are not optional: every backend has them. Networking has its finer-grained report, `Net.Support.current`.

entries.name: BACKEND
entries.summary:
Which backend is executing this program.

Its `interpreted?`, `compiled?` and `beam?` are the readable way to ask.

entries.name: Version
entries.summary:
Build identity for the compiler and runtime executing this program: `Version` and `VERSION` below.

Useful in bug reports, generated artifacts, and compatibility checks where `Kex.BACKEND` alone is not enough to identify the toolchain. The toolchain a program is running on. `kex --version` and the REPL banner report the same numbers.

`revision` is the git commit the compiler was built from: `None` when it was built from a source archive rather than a checkout, which is why it is an Optional rather than a String.

entries.name: tuple
entries.summary:
The version's four values as a tuple, for destructuring.

A tuple cannot carry accessors of its own: there is no named type for a `make` block to target, so the record is the value and this is the view.

entries.name: release
entries.summary:
The three numbers, plus the pre-release channel when there is one.

`0.4.0`, or `0.4.0-rc.1` on a pre-release build. What a version RANGE is matched against, so the channel has to be in it.

entries.name: number
entries.summary:
The release string with the build revision after it, when there is one.

This is what `kex --version` and the REPL banner print.

`to(String)`: the language's conversion protocol, and what this should really be: is deliberately NOT defined here: a second `to(String)` implementation anywhere in the prelude breaks type-directed `to` dispatch for every prelude type on BEAM, so adding one here silently broke `3.kilo.watt.to(String)`. Pinned by spec/prelude_to_string_dispatch.kex; restore this as `to(String)` once that dispatcher is fixed.

entries.name: VERSION
entries.summary: This build's version.

entries.name: Kex.Feature
entries.summary:
Which optional capabilities this build includes.

Optional non-network capabilities in this build. Networking has its own granular opt-in `Net.Support` report.

entries.name: has?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when this build includes `f`.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: Every optional capability this build includes.

entries.name: Kex.Interface
entries.summary: Reading the typed public surface of a compiled Kex module.

entries.name: read
entries.summary:
Reads the KexI interface chunk of a compiled Kex module: its typed public surface, and answers the decoded term, or None when the file has no such chunk, does not exist, or is not a BEAM artifact.

The term is an ordinary tree of tuples, lists, atoms, integers and strings, so it is walked with normal pattern matching and `Tuple.items`. This exists so that reading it needs no `BEAM.*` interop: it is the one intentional entry point rather than a general term decoder.

entries.name: inspected
entries.summary:
Returns the pretty-printed representation of any value as a STRING: the same form the REPL echoes. Universal: reachable on every type through UFCS.

Named apart from `inspect`, which prints and returns its INPUT so it can be dropped into a pipeline. Both spellings used to be called `inspect`, and which one a call reached depended on whether it was written `x.inspect` or `IO.inspect(x)`, so `[1, 2].inspect.count` answered 24, the length of the rendered string, rather than 2.

entries.name: inspect
entries.summary: Prints the pretty-printed form of `value` to stderr and returns `value` unchanged, so it can be dropped into any pipeline without changing what flows through it. The same operation as `IO.inspect`, reachable by UFCS.

entries.name: List
entries.summary:
An ordered, immutable sequence, written [1, 2, 3].

Lists are the default collection in Kex. Every operation answers with a new list rather than changing the receiver, so a chain of transformations is safe to read from either end.

```kex
let scores = [7, 2, 9, 4]
scores.filter { |n| n > 3 }      # => [7, 9, 4]
scores.sort                      # => [2, 4, 7, 9]
scores.map { |n| n * 10 }.sum    # => 220
```

Anything that might not be there: the first element, an element at an index, a search result: answers with an `Optional`, so an empty list is an ordinary case rather than a crash:

```kex
[].first.or(0)        # => 0
[1, 2].at(9).or(0)    # => 0
```

A list is `Enumerable` and `Foldable`, which is where `map`, `filter`, `find`, `all?` and `reduce` come from.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Sums all elements. Returns `0` for an empty list.

entries.name: product
entries.summary: Multiplies all elements. Returns `1` for an empty list.

entries.name: product
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` and multiplies the results.

entries.name: min
entries.summary: Returns the smallest element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list.

entries.name: max
entries.summary: Returns the largest element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list.

entries.name: flatten
entries.summary: Flattens exactly one level of nesting.

entries.name: [X]
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> X -> A)) -> A

entries.name: first
entries.summary: Returns the first element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list is empty.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns the second element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list has fewer than two elements.

entries.name: third
entries.summary: Returns the third element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list has fewer than three elements.

entries.name: rest
entries.summary: Returns all elements after the first. Returns `[]` for an empty or single-element list.

entries.name: last
entries.summary: Returns the last element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list is empty.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of elements. When given a predicate, returns the count of elements for which it holds.

entries.name: length
entries.summary: Returns the number of elements. The same as `count`, under the name `String` uses.

entries.name: count
entries.summary:
Returns how many elements satisfy `pred`.

count(pred) is provided by the Enumerable trait.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if the list contains no elements.

entries.name: find
entries.summary:
Returns the first element satisfying the predicate wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if no element matches.

find/any?/all? are provided by the Enumerable trait.

entries.name: any?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if at least one element satisfies the predicate.

entries.name: all?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if every element satisfies the predicate.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Transforms each element by applying `f`.

map/filter/each are provided by the Enumerable trait (in terms of reduce).

entries.name: filter
entries.summary: Returns a new list containing only the elements for which `pred` is `true`.

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns a new list with all elements for which `pred` is `true` removed. The inverse of `filter`.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each element for its side effects. Returns unit.

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> X -> A)) -> A
entries.summary: Folds the list from the left, starting with `acc` and combining each element via `f`.

entries.name: flatMap
entries.summary: Maps each element to a list and concatenates the results.

entries.name: at
entries.summary: Returns the element at position `i` (0-based) wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the index is out of range.

entries.name: get
entries.summary: Returns the element at position `i` (0-based), or `None` when the index is out of range. The same as `at`.

entries.name: contains?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if `elem` is present in the list.

entries.name: indexOf
entries.summary: Returns `true` if the first index at which `elem` appears, wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the element is not present.

entries.name: findIndex
entries.summary: Returns the index of the first element satisfying `pred`, wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if none does. The predicate counterpart of `indexOf`, which searches by value.

entries.name: takeWhile
entries.summary: Returns the longest leading run of elements satisfying `pred`. Stops at the first element that does not, so it is not `filter`: later matches are dropped with everything after the first failure.

entries.name: dropWhile
entries.summary: Returns what is left after `takeWhile`: everything from the first element that does not satisfy `pred` onwards.

entries.name: uniq
entries.summary: Returns a new list with duplicate elements removed, preserving the first occurrence of each element.

entries.name: partition
entries.summary: Splits the list into two lists: those for which `pred` is `true` (first) and those for which it is `false` (second).

entries.name: collect
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` (which returns an `Optional`), keeping and unwrapping the `Just(y)` results and dropping `None`. Filter + map fused.

entries.name: take
entries.summary: Returns the first `n` elements.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary: Drops the first `n` elements.

entries.name: push
entries.summary: Returns a new list with `x` appended at the end.

entries.name: reverse
entries.summary: Returns the elements in reverse order.

entries.name: zip
entries.summary: Pairs each element of this list with the corresponding element of `other`. Stops at the end of the shorter list.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements sorted in ascending natural order.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements sorted using a custom comparator. `comp` should return `true` when its first argument should come before its second.

entries.name: min
entries.summary: Returns the element with the smallest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list.

entries.name: max
entries.summary: Returns the element with the largest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` and sums the results.

entries.name: join
entries.summary:
Renders and concatenates the elements, placing `sep` between adjacent values. With no separator, the rendered values are joined directly.

Elements do not have to be strings: each is rendered using the same user-facing conversion used by interpolation and printing.

entries.name: Map
entries.summary: Declared for the same reason list.kex declares `type List<X> = [X]`: it gives the name `Map` a source declaration, so it resolves as a type through the collected interfaces rather than needing to be known to the compiler.

entries.name: Map<K, V>
signatures: reduce(acc: A, g: (A -> (K, V) -> A)) -> A
put(k: K, v: V) -> Map<K, V>

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, g: (A -> (K, V) -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Folds over the map's `(key, value)` pairs in canonical key order.

This is `Map`'s `Enumerable` primitive: `map`, `filter`, `find`, `any?` and the rest are built on it. The block receives the accumulator and one pair; destructure the pair to name its halves.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: The empty map: the identity element of the `Monoid` instance, so `m.combine({})` is `m`.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Combines two maps by merging them, with `other`'s values winning on a key conflict. The `Monoid` operation, and the same thing `merge` does.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Returns the value stored under `key`, or `None` when the key is absent.

Missing keys are an ordinary answer rather than a failure, so a lookup on data you did not produce is safe by default. Use the two-argument form below when you have a sensible fallback.

entries.name: put
signatures: put(k: K, v: V) -> Map<K, V>
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with `key` mapped to `value`, replacing any previous entry for that key.

The receiver is untouched. Use `put!` when you want the variable holding the map to be rebound to the result.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary:
Returns a new map without `key`. A key that is not present is not an error: the map comes back unchanged.

Use `delete!` to rebind the receiver variable.

entries.name: has?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `key` has an entry in the map.

Distinguishes a missing key from one whose value is itself empty, which a `get` with a default cannot.

entries.name: empty?
