entries.summary: Returns `true` when the map has no entries.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of entries.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of entries satisfying `pred`.

entries.name: keys
entries.summary: Returns the map's keys as a list, in canonical key order.

entries.name: values
entries.summary: Returns the map's values as a list, ordered by their keys.

entries.name: entries
entries.summary:
Returns the map's entries as a list of `(key, value)` tuples, in canonical key order.

This is the bridge to the `List` methods a map does not have of its own, and the form the two-parameter blocks elsewhere are splatting from.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each key and value, for its side effects.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each key and value and collects the results into a LIST.

Note the return type: `map` comes from `Enumerable`, whose contract is to produce a list, because `f` may return anything at all. Use `mapValues` or `mapKeys` when you want a map back.

entries.name: mapValues
entries.summary: Returns a new map with every value replaced by `f(value)`. The keys are left alone.

entries.name: mapKeys
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with every key replaced by `f(key)`. The values are left alone.

If `f` maps two keys onto the same result, one entry wins: the map cannot hold both.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with only the entries for which `pred` answers `true`.

Map overrides the map-returning HOFs (Enumerable's default returns a list).

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns a new map with the entries for which `pred` answers `true` removed. The complement of `filter`.

entries.name: merge
entries.summary:
Returns a new map holding the entries of both. When a key appears in both, `other`'s value wins.

The right-biased rule is what makes this the natural way to apply overrides on top of defaults.

entries.name: any?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when at least one entry satisfies `pred`. Stops at the first match.

entries.name: all?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when every entry satisfies `pred`. The empty map answers `true`.

entries.name: find
entries.summary:
Returns the first entry satisfying `pred` as a `(key, value)` tuple, or `None` when nothing matches.

"First" means first in canonical key order.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the map has no entries. The `Blankable` view of `empty?`, so a map can be tested by the same generic code that tests strings and lists.

entries.name: Math
entries.summary:
Mathematical constants and functions.

All trigonometric functions work in radians. Every function here accepts a `Number` (an `Integer` or a `Float`) and the transcendental ones answer with a `Float`.

A Kex `Float` is always finite, so a domain error (`Math.sqrt(-1.0)`) or an overflow (`Math.exp(1000.0)`) raises rather than producing `NaN` or `Infinity`: the same rule the BEAM enforces, where those two values cannot exist at all. There is no non-finite float to test for afterwards.

```kex
Math.sqrt(2.0)              # => 1.4142135623730951
Math.hypot(3.0, 4.0)        # => 5.0
Math.sin(Math.PI / 2.0)     # => 1.0
```

The everyday operations on a single number: `abs`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `sqrt`: are also methods on `Integer` and `Float`, which usually reads better in a chain: `x.abs` over `Math.abs(x)`.

entries.name: PI
entries.summary: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.

entries.name: E
entries.summary: The base of the natural logarithm.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary: Returns the square root of `x`. Raises for a negative `x`, which has no real root.

entries.name: cbrt
entries.summary: Returns the cube root of `x`. Unlike `sqrt`, negative input is fine: a negative number has a real cube root.

entries.name: sin
entries.summary: Returns the sine of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: cos
entries.summary: Returns the cosine of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: tan
entries.summary: Returns the tangent of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: asin
entries.summary: Returns the arc sine of `x` in radians, in the range -π/2 to π/2.

entries.name: acos
entries.summary: Returns the arc cosine of `x` in radians, in the range 0 to π.

entries.name: atan
entries.summary:
Returns the arc tangent of `x` in radians, in the range -π/2 to π/2.

Use `atan2` when you have both coordinates of a vector: it can tell the quadrant apart, and this cannot.

entries.name: atan2
entries.summary:
Returns the angle of the vector `(x, y)` in radians, from -π to π.

Both signs are taken into account, so the result lands in the correct quadrant, which is why this, not `atan`, is what you want for converting a vector to an angle. Note the argument order: `y` first.

entries.name: sinh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic sine of `x`.

entries.name: cosh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cosine of `x`.

entries.name: tanh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of `x`, always between -1 and 1.

entries.name: log
entries.summary:
Returns the natural logarithm of `x`: its logarithm to base `e`. With a second argument, returns the logarithm to that base instead.

Raises for `x` of zero or less, which has no real logarithm.

entries.name: log2
entries.summary: Returns the base-2 logarithm of `x`. The same as `Math.log(x, 2.0)`, and more direct.

entries.name: log10
entries.summary: Returns the base-10 logarithm of `x`.

entries.name: exp
entries.summary:
Returns `e` raised to the power `x`: the inverse of `Math.log`.

Raises on overflow, which for a double happens a little past `x` of 709.

entries.name: pow
entries.summary:
Returns `x` raised to the power `y`.

The result is always a `Float`, even for whole arguments, so round it when you need an integer back.

entries.name: abs
entries.summary:
Returns the magnitude of `x`, discarding its sign. The type is preserved: an `Integer` in gives an `Integer` out.

`x.abs` is the same thing as a method, and usually reads better.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the largest integer that is not greater than `x`: rounding toward negative infinity.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the smallest integer that is not less than `x`: rounding toward positive infinity.

entries.name: hypot
entries.summary: Returns the Euclidean distance +sqrt(x*x + y*y)+, computed so that large values do not overflow on the way.

entries.name: Reader
entries.summary:
Mock: deterministic stand-ins for the world outside the program: the filesystem, environment, and console. Networking mocks live under Mock.Net.

These are STATEFUL: `Mock.FS.File(path, content)` writes into a store the real `FS.File` then reads back, so a test can write and read again, and `clear()` undoes it. That state is global and lives until cleared, which is what makes hook ordering and write/read round trips testable, and also what makes two tests able to interfere.

When a test only needs canned ANSWERS, replacing the capability is the better tool: `with FS.File = MyFake { ... } do ... end` swaps the implementation for one lexical region, holds no global state, needs no clearing, and cannot leak into another test. See spec/capability_stdlib_fs.kex for the shape of a stand-in (kexhq/kex#143).

Opt-in on purpose (issue #144): this module used to ride along inside a prelude networking file, so importing the prelude made every Mock.* reachable from every program without anyone asking for it. Reachable is still not callable: the runtime denies the mock intrinsics outside spec files, the REPL, and --allow-mocks, but it should also not be in scope by accident. A qualified `Mock.FS.File(...)` auto-loads this file like any other opt-in module.

All Mock.* sub-modules live in a single `module Mock` block so merged compilation units never see duplicate top-level `Mock` modules. A stand-in's read hook: a path in, its content or `None` out.

entries.name: Lookup
entries.summary: An environment stand-in's lookup hook: a name in, its value or `None` out.

entries.name: Writer
entries.summary: An environment stand-in's WRITE hook: the name and the value a program set. A `Mock.Env` is an immutable record, so a write cannot land in its `vars`, and it must not reach the real environment, or a test would leak a variable into the next one and into anything the suite starts. The hook is how a test observes the write instead: record it, assert on it, or ignore it, which is what `None` does.

entries.name: Files
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `FS.File` capability, for `with FS.File = ...`. Unlike the `Mock.*` functions below it holds no global state, needs no `clear()`, and cannot leak past its block. What it cannot do is change: `write` then `read` back is not something a value does, so a test needing that round trip still wants `Mock.FS` (kexhq/kex#143).

```kex
with FS.File = Mock.Files { files: {"kex.toml": "name = \"demo\""} } do
  assert(loadConfig() == "demo")
end
```

`onRead` takes over when a test needs an ANSWER rather than a fixture: content derived from the path, a failure on the third call, a record of what was asked for. It is consulted first and its `None` means "no such file", so a callback can model absence too.

entries.name: Env
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `ENV` capability. A name simply left out of `vars` reads as unset, which is the whole reason `Mock.ENV.unset` exists: absence is an answer programs act on. `onGet` answers instead of the map when a test wants a rule rather than a fixture.

```kex
with ENV = Mock.Env { vars: {"HOME": "/fake"} } do
  assert(configHome() == "/fake/.config")
end
```

entries.name: Mock.FS
entries.summary:
A stateful stand-in for the filesystem: files a test declares, that the real `FS.File` then reads back.

The store is global and lives until `clear`, which is what makes a write followed by a read testable, and what makes two tests able to interfere. Clear it in an `after` hook.

```kex
describe "the config loader" do
  before do
    Mock.FS.files({ "app.conf": "port = 8080\n" })
  end

  after do
    Mock.FS.clear()
  end

  it "reads the port" do
    Assert.equal(loadPort(), 8080)
  end
end
```

entries.name: File
entries.summary: Declares one file and its content.

entries.name: Directory
entries.summary: Declares a directory at `path`.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Empties the store, so nothing declared so far is visible any more.

Call it in an `after` hook: the store is global, and what one test leaves behind the next one sees.

entries.name: files
entries.summary:
Declares the whole fixture in one call.

The same shape `Mock.Files { files: ... }` takes: one line instead of one per file (kexhq/kex#143).

entries.name: onRead
entries.summary:
Answers reads by RULE rather than from a fixture.

Content derived from the path, a failure on the third call, a record of what was asked for. Consulted before the map, and returning `None` means "no such file", so absence is expressible too.

entries.name: Mock.ENV
entries.summary:
Overlays the process environment, so a test can say what `ENV` holds instead of depending on how it was launched.

The overlay is global and lives until `clear`: clear it in an `after` hook.

```kex
Mock.ENV.vars({ "HOME": "/fake", "LOG_LEVEL": "debug" })
assert(configPath() == "/fake/.config")
Mock.ENV.clear()
```

entries.name: set
entries.summary: Sets one variable in the overlay.

entries.name: unset
entries.summary:
Removes one variable from the overlay, so it reads as unset.

Separate from `set` because a variable being ABSENT is an answer programs act on, and there is no value that means it.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary: Removes the whole overlay, restoring the real environment.

entries.name: vars
entries.summary:
Declares the whole overlay in one call.

The same shape `Mock.Env { vars: ... }` takes (kexhq/kex#143). There is no `onGet` here: global `ENV` is a materialised Map, so there is nothing for a callback to intercept: use `with ENV = Mock.Env { onGet: ... }` when a rule is what you want.

entries.name: Mock.IO
entries.summary:
A stateful stand-in for the console: captures what a program prints, and feeds it lines as if they had been typed.

The way to test a program that talks to a person without one being there.

```kex
Mock.IO.start()
Mock.IO.input("Ada", "42")
greet()
Assert.equal(Mock.IO.output(), "hello, Ada\n")
Mock.IO.stop()
```

entries.name: start
entries.summary: Starts capturing output and serving queued input.

entries.name: stop
entries.summary: Stops capturing, and restores the real console.

entries.name: output
entries.summary:
Everything the program has printed since capturing started.

Newlines are included, so a single `IO.printLine("hi")` gives `"hi\n"`.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Discards the captured output, while continuing to capture.

Useful between phases of one test, when only the later output matters.

entries.name: input
entries.summary:
Queues the lines `IO.getLine` will return, in order.

Takes a list, or up to four lines as separate arguments. Once they run out, `IO.getLine` answers `None`: end of input, exactly as a closed stdin would.

entries.name: cannedRead
entries.summary: Named apart from `read`: `this.read(path)` would bind to the capability's own `read : FilePath -> String?`, not to this method.

entries.name: open
entries.summary: A fake is a value, so there is nowhere for a write to go. Refusing is the honest answer and the useful one: a test that did not expect a write sees it fail rather than silently succeed.

entries.name: lookup
entries.summary: Named apart from `get`: `this.get(key)` would bind to the capability's own `get`, not to this method.

entries.name: set
entries.summary: A write goes to `onSet` or nowhere. It must NOT reach the real environment: a substituted ENV is the whole point of the mock, and a test that set a variable would otherwise leak it into the next one and into every process the suite starts. `vars` cannot take it either: a record is immutable, so a test that cares about writes supplies the hook, and one that does not gets a write that goes quietly nowhere.

entries.name: Mock.Net
entries.summary: Scriptable networking values are namespaced so importing Mock does not recreate any of the removed global HTTP types.

entries.name: Mock.Net.HTTP
entries.summary: Canned HTTP transport state for networking specifications.

entries.name: Transport
entries.summary: Responses returned in order by a scripted transport.

entries.name: Mock.Net.DNS
entries.summary: Canned DNS resolver state for networking specifications.

entries.name: ResolverScript
entries.summary: Hostname-to-address answers supplied without touching the network.

entries.name: Mock.Net.Socket
entries.summary: Canned byte-stream state for socket specifications.

entries.name: Script
entries.summary: Binary chunks delivered in order as incoming socket data.

entries.name: Mock.Net.WebSocket
entries.summary: Canned message state for WebSocket specifications.

entries.name: Script
entries.summary: High-level messages delivered in order by a scripted connection.

entries.name: Net
entries.summary:
Shared networking values, capability discovery, and typed failures.

```kex
using Net

let https = Port.from(443).try
if Support.current.tls.usable? then https.string else "TLS unavailable" end
```

entries.name: Port
entries.summary:
A validated TCP or UDP port number in `0..65535`.

Use `Port.from` at input boundaries. Port zero requests an ephemeral port where a listening API permits it; after binding, ask the server or socket for the concrete port the operating system chose.

entries.name: SupportValue
entries.summary:
Whether a feature was compiled into this backend and is usable now.

`compiled?` describes the build; `usable?` also accounts for the environment it is running in. A browser build may contain an HTTP client, for example, while browser policy still prevents a particular lower-level capability.

entries.name: SupportReport
entries.summary:
Granular networking capabilities for the current backend and environment.

Read this before choosing a transport dynamically. Applications that require one capability can instead check that single field during startup and fail with a useful message.

entries.name: Net.Port
entries.summary: Validated `Port` construction.

entries.name: from
entries.summary: Validates a port number.

entries.name: Net.Support
entries.summary: Runtime discovery for optional network transports and protocols.

entries.name: current
entries.summary: Reports compiled and currently usable networking features.

entries.name: NetOperation
entries.summary: The subsystem or operation that produced a networking error.

entries.name: NetErrorKind
entries.summary: Stable, backend-independent networking failure categories.

entries.name: NetError
entries.summary:
A typed networking failure shared by every network module.

`kind` is the stable category to branch on. `message` is for a person, while `phase` adds protocol context such as a TLS handshake and `progress` records bytes transferred before a partial-operation failure. Keeping those roles separate lets programs recover without matching backend-specific prose.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Renders the decimal port without a host or scheme.

entries.name: Node
entries.summary:
Distributed Kex: this BEAM node, and the other nodes it is connected to.

A node is one running BEAM VM with a name. Once two nodes share a cookie and are connected, a `Pid` from one works on the other: `send`, `link` and `monitor` cross the network unchanged, and so do typed `Process` and `Server` handles.

Name a node when starting it (`kex --sname a --cookie secret app.kex`), or from inside the program with `Node.start`:

```kex
using Node

main do
  Node.connect(:b@myhost)
  Node.send(:b@myhost, :logger, (:hello, Node.self))
end
```

Node names are atoms: `:b@myhost` for a short name, the quoted `:"b@host.example.com"` for one with dots, or `Atom.from(text)` for one built at runtime.

Both nodes need the same compiled code for anything that carries a function, like a lambda or a record whose methods the receiver calls; `Node.spawn` sends its block's code along. Plain data — numbers, strings, lists, tuples, records — needs nothing.

Backed by Kex.Intrinsic.Node on the BEAM. The tree-walk interpreter is always a single, unnamed node.

entries.name: self
entries.summary: This node's name, or `:nonode@nohost` when it is not distributed.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary: Whether this node is distributed — started with a name, so other nodes can connect to it.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: The nodes this one is currently connected to, not including itself.

entries.name: start
entries.summary: Makes this node distributed under `name`, as `--sname`/`--name` would at startup. A `name` whose host has a dot (`:"app@host.example.com"`) uses long names; anything else uses short names.

entries.name: stop
entries.summary: Stops distribution: the node drops its name and every connection.

entries.name: connect
entries.summary: Connects to the node named `node`. Both nodes must share a cookie.

entries.name: disconnect
entries.summary: Drops the connection to `node`.

entries.name: setCookie
entries.summary: Sets the cookie this node presents when connecting. Nodes connect only when their cookies match.

entries.name: send
entries.summary: Sends `message` to the process registered as `name` on `node`, unchanged. Like `Pid.send`, it never blocks and never fails.

entries.name: whereIs
entries.summary: The `Pid` registered as `name` on `node`, or `None`.

entries.name: spawn
entries.summary:
Runs `block` in a new process on `node` and returns its `Pid`.

The block is a function of THIS program. When `node` has not loaded the module it belongs to, that module's compiled code is sent over and loaded first. A module `node` already has is left as it is.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
Whole numbers, of arbitrary size.

`Integer` has no width limit: factorials and cryptographic moduli are ordinary values, not a special big-number type you have to opt into.

`Integer` and `Float` are one numeric tower: they compare and order across the boundary, so `0 == 0.0` is `true` and `[1, 2.5, 3].sort` works. What differs is the arithmetic. `/` on two integers is integer division, and `sqrt` answers a `Float` because a square root generally is one.

```kex
7 / 2          # => 3      (integer division)
7.0 / 2.0      # => 3.5
16.sqrt        # => 4.0    (a Float, even from an Integer)
(-7).modulo(3) # => 2      (mathematical modulo, not C remainder)
```

entries.name: even?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer is divisible by two. Zero is even, and negative numbers follow the same rule.

entries.name: odd?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer is not divisible by two. The opposite of `even?`.

entries.name: abs
entries.summary: Returns the magnitude of the integer, discarding its sign.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary:
Returns the square root as a `Float`.

The result is a `Float` even when the root is exact, because in general it is not. Round or floor it when you need an integer back.

entries.name: modulo
entries.summary:
Returns `this` modulo `n`.

The result takes the sign of `n`, which is mathematical modulo rather than the C-style remainder other languages give. That is what makes it safe for wrapping an index that may have gone negative.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: times
entries.summary:
Calls `f` exactly `this` times, passing the 0-based iteration index.

This is the counting loop. When you want the numbers themselves rather than a count of repetitions, `(1..n).items.each` often reads better.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. Present so that code written against `Number` works whichever half of the tower it is handed.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. The `Integer` counterpart of `Float.ceil`.

entries.name: round
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. The `Integer` counterpart of `Float.round`.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary:
Double-precision floating-point numbers.

A Kex `Float` is always finite. An operation that would produce `NaN` or `Infinity` raises instead: the same rule the BEAM enforces, where those two values cannot exist at all. So a `Float` you are holding is always a real number, and there is no `nan?` to check for.

`Float` and `Integer` compare and order across the boundary; see `Integer` for the rest of the numeric tower.

```kex
3.7.floor      # => 3
3.7.round      # => 4
(-3.7).toInteger  # => -3   (truncates toward zero)
```

entries.name: abs
entries.summary: Returns the magnitude of the float, discarding its sign.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary: Returns the square root. Raises for a negative receiver, which has no real root.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the float falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the largest integer that is not greater than the float: it always rounds toward negative infinity, which is what separates it from `toInteger` for negative values.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the smallest integer that is not less than the float: it always rounds toward positive infinity.

entries.name: round
entries.summary: Returns the nearest integer, with halves rounding away from zero.

entries.name: toInteger
entries.summary: Truncates toward zero and returns the result as an `Integer`: it drops the fractional part rather than rounding, so it differs from both `floor` and `round` for negative values.

entries.name: Integer
signatures: parse(s: String, radix: Integer) -> Result<Integer, ParseError>
entries.summary:
Reading integers out of text.

Use `parse` when a failure needs explaining and `"42".to(Integer)` when it does not: `to` answers a plain `Optional`, `parse` answers a `Result` carrying a `ParseError` that says where it stopped and what it had read so far.

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(s: String, radix: Integer) -> Result<Integer, ParseError>
entries.summary:
Parses the whole string as a base-10 integer.

The string must be entirely consumed: leading or trailing characters make it an `Error`, with a `ParseError` describing where parsing stopped. Use `parsePrefix` when a trailing remainder is expected.

entries.name: parsePrefix
entries.summary:
Parses an integer from the front of the string and returns it together with whatever text was left over.

This is the building block for hand-written scanners: parse a number, keep going from the remainder. Answers `None` when the string does not begin with a number at all.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary: Reading floating-point numbers out of text.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses the whole string as a float.

The string must be entirely consumed; anything left over makes it an `Error` carrying a `ParseError`.

entries.name: parsePrefix
entries.summary: Parses a float from the front of the string and returns it together with the unconsumed remainder. Answers `None` when the string does not begin with a number.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary:
The largest finite `Float`.

A Kex `Float` is always finite, so there is no infinity to start from: this is the bound to use instead, say as the first "smallest so far".

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite `Float`: `-Float.MAX`. Not the smallest positive one, which some languages call MIN.

entries.name: Float32
entries.summary:
The bounds of the sized numeric types: `Int8.MAX`, `UInt64.MAX`, `Float32.MIN` and so on. `Integer` has none: it is arbitrary-precision. For a float type, `MIN` is the most negative finite value, not the smallest positive one.

The range of a 32-bit float.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Float32: 3.4028234663852886e38.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite Float32: -3.4028234663852886e38.

entries.name: Float64
entries.summary: The range of a 64-bit float, the same as a `Float`.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite Float64: -1.7976931348623157e308.

entries.name: Int8
entries.summary: The range of a signed 8-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int8: 127.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int8: -128.

entries.name: Int16
entries.summary: The range of a signed 16-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int16: 32767.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int16: -32768.

entries.name: Int32
entries.summary: The range of a signed 32-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int32: 2147483647.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int32: -2147483648.

entries.name: Int64
entries.summary: The range of a signed 64-bit integer.

entries.name: UInt8
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 8-bit integer: `UInt8` is another name for `Byte`.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt8: 255.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt8: 0.

entries.name: UInt16
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 16-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt16: 65535.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt16: 0.

entries.name: UInt32
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 32-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt32: 4294967295.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt32: 0.

entries.name: UInt64
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 64-bit integer.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt64: 0.

entries.name: Byte
entries.summary: The range of a `Byte`, Kex's unsigned 8-bit integer (also called `UInt8`).

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Byte: 255.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Byte: 0.

entries.name: Number
entries.summary: Reading a number out of text without deciding in advance which half of the numeric tower it belongs to.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses the whole string as an `Integer` or a `Float`, whichever the text describes.

Use it when the input's shape is not known ahead of time: a config value, a CSV column that may hold either.

entries.name: Optional
entries.summary:
An optional value: `Just(x)` carries a value, `None` says there is none.

`X?` is shorthand for `Optional<X>`, and is the spelling you will normally write. Kex has no `null`: anything that might not produce a value returns an `Optional` instead, so the compiler makes you say what happens when it is empty. Most of the time that is a single `.or(default)` at the end of a chain.

Pattern matching handles the cases that need more than a default:

entries.name: Result
entries.summary:
The outcome of an operation that can fail: `Ok(x)` on success, `Error(e)` on failure with a reason.

Use `Result` over `Optional` when the *reason* for failure matters to the caller. Parsing is the standard example: `"12x".to(Integer)` answers `None`, while `Integer.parse("12x")` answers an `Error` that says where it stopped.

entries.name: Either
entries.summary:
One of two values, of possibly different types: `Left(l)` or `Right(r)`.

Unlike `Result`, neither side means failure: `Either` is for a value that is legitimately one of two shapes.

entries.name: Optionable
entries.summary:
A value that may be absent. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any optional value.

The two operations below are what make the constraint worth having: an empty trait would accept a value and then let you do nothing with it, since there would be no method to call. `map` is deliberately NOT required — its result type differs per implementer (`Y?` here, `Result<Y, E>` for `Resultable`), which needs a higher-kinded parameter Kex does not have.

entries.name: set?
entries.summary:
Answers `true` when a value is present.

The one operation an `Optionable` type must define; `none?` is its negation.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the wrapped value, or `default` when there is none.

The way out of the optional world, and the reason a constrained parameter is usable at all.

entries.name: Resultable
entries.summary: A value that either succeeded or failed with a reason. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any result value.

entries.name: ok?
entries.summary:
Answers `true` for a success.

The one operation a `Resultable` type must define; `error?` is its negation.

entries.name: or
entries.summary: Returns the success value, or `default` on failure.

entries.name: Eitherable
entries.summary: One of two values, neither meaning failure. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any either value.

entries.name: either
entries.summary:
Case analysis: applies `onLeft` to a `Left` and `onRight` to a `Right`.

The one operation an `Eitherable` type must define — `left?` and `right?` are both written in terms of it. A discriminator alone would let you ask which side a value is on without being able to reach it, which is why this is the requirement rather than those.

entries.name: set?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when a value is present.

entries.name: none?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when there is no value. The opposite of `set?`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the wrapped value, or `default` when there is none.

This is the usual way an optional leaves the optional world: put `.or` at the end of a chain and the rest of your code works with a plain value.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the wrapped value, keeping the result wrapped. `None` is returned unchanged, so `f` never sees a missing value.

entries.name: flatMap
entries.summary:
Applies `f`, which itself returns an optional, and flattens the result.

Use it instead of `map` when the step can also fail: `map` would give you a doubly wrapped `Just(Just(x))`, `flatMap` gives a single layer. A `None` anywhere in the chain short-circuits the rest.

entries.name: ok?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the result is `Ok`.

entries.name: error?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the result is `Error`. The opposite of `ok?`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the `Ok` value, or `default` when the result is an `Error`.

The error payload is discarded. Match on the result instead when you need to report why it failed.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the `Ok` value. An `Error` passes through untouched, so a chain of `map` calls describes the success path only.

entries.name: flatMap
entries.summary:
Applies `f`, which itself returns a `Result`, and flattens the result.

The step-by-step form of `map` for stages that can fail on their own. The first `Error` ends the chain and is the answer.

entries.name: optional
entries.summary:
Converts the result to an `Optional`, dropping the error payload.

Useful when a caller only needs to know whether there is a value, and everything downstream already speaks `Optional`.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(value, t: Type, radix: Integer) -> A?
entries.summary:
Converts `value` to the type `t`, or `None` if it cannot be represented.

`t` is a runtime type value: write the type name itself: `String`, `Integer`, `Float`, `List`. Conversion to `String` goes through the `Showable` protocol, so it works for every value.

The result is an `Optional`, not a `Result`, and deliberately so: the reason a conversion failed is usually implied by the types alone. When the reason carries information (where a parse gave up and on what) reach for `Integer.parse` or `Float.parse`, which answer with `Result<_, ParseError>`. So: `to` for every day, `parse` when the failure needs handling.

entries.name: either
entries.summary:
Case analysis: applies `onLeft` to a `Left` and `onRight` to a `Right`.

The way an `Either` is consumed without a `match`, and the operation `Eitherable` requires. Both branches answer the same type, so the result is a plain value rather than another `Either`.

entries.name: left?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Left`.

entries.name: right?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Right`. The opposite of `left?`.

entries.name: OptionKind
entries.summary: What kind of value an option carries: `StringValue` takes any text, `IntegerValue` must parse as a number, and `FlagValue` takes none at all and reads as `"true"` when present.

entries.name: OptionSpec
entries.summary: One declared option. Built for you by the `OptionConfig` builders: you rarely construct one by hand.

entries.name: CommandHandler
entries.summary: What a command does once the line has been parsed. It receives the parsed options with the command's own words already removed, so `tey add greet` hands its handler `["greet"]`, and returns the process exit code.

entries.name: CommandSpec
entries.summary: One declared command. Built for you by the `OptionConfig.command` builders.

entries.name: OptionConfig
entries.summary:
A tool's whole command-line interface: its name, its options, and its commands.

Build one with `OptionParser.define` and add to it with the chainable `string`, `integer`, `flag` and `command` methods. Each returns a new `OptionConfig`, so the chain reads as one declaration.

entries.name: ParsedOptions
entries.summary: The result of a successful parse: the option values, and the words that were not options.

entries.name: OptionParseError
entries.summary:
Why a command line could not be parsed.

`OptionParser.errorMessage` turns one into a sentence for the user; `OptionConfig.run` does that for you.

entries.name: value
entries.summary: Returns the value given for the option named `name`, or `None` when it was neither supplied nor defaulted.

entries.name: flagEnabled?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the flag named `name` was given.

entries.name: integerValue
entries.summary:
Returns the value of an integer option as an `Integer`, or `None` when it is absent or does not parse.

An option declared with `integer` has already been checked at parse time, so `None` here means absent rather than malformed.

entries.name: OptionConfig
signatures: string(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
integer(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
flag(long: String, short: Char?, description: String) -> OptionConfig
command(name: String, usage: String, description: String, section: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
